- **Introduction:** problem, motivation, one concrete example, and 1-2 bounded contributions.
- **Related Work:** 3-7 verified IEEE-style references listed in §2 and 1-3 alternatives with a brief rationale.
- **Method:** approach, pipeline, versioned tools, 2-3 design decisions, and configuration including seeds and environment.
- **Experiments:** one or more numbered experiment subsections, each with setup and results. Include the dataset, protocol, baseline comparison, and specific verification within those template fields without adding separate headings that are absent from the template.
- **Discussion:** a real failure, root cause, fix and confirmation, what worked, and what did not or surprised the student.
- **AI Usage Disclosure:** every AI tool and use, what the student personally verified, what remained unverified, and a reference to the authentic session log.
- **References:** keep the template's pointer to the numbered references in §2 rather than duplicating the bibliography.

The sample report is a layout and writing example only. Do not copy its facts or its deviations from the binding rules: it omits the title-block email, a distinct `How AI was used` item, a `What I trusted without verification` item, and the `session.json` reference, and it uses six index terms instead of the allowed 3-5.

- their own interpretation and alternative considered;
- at least one verification they personally performed;
- what they trusted without verification;
- the exact AI tools and uses reflected in the authentic session log.

If confirmation is missing, retain an explicit review marker or disclose that the item was not personally verified. Do not silently convert agent work into a first-person student claim.

## Require confirmation before PDF

Finish and validate the Markdown report before creating the PDF. Give the student the path to the `.md` file and wait for explicit confirmation that its content is approved. Do not create, render, or update the PDF before that confirmation.

After confirmation, render the approved Markdown to PDF without making undisclosed substantive changes. If conversion requires a content change, update the Markdown source first and obtain confirmation again.

Then inspect every PDF page for clipped text, unreadable figures, broken links, overflow, and accidental inclusion of review markers. Verify that the body occupies no more than 5 pages unless the weekly sheet says otherwise.

## Prepare the submission pair

Before confirmation, the report artifact is:

- `<student-id-or-name>_<assignment-id>_report.md`

After the student confirms that Markdown report, create or identify exactly these submission artifacts:

- `<student-id-or-name>_<assignment-id>_report.pdf`
- `<student-id-or-name>_<assignment-id>_session.json`

The session file must be the full, unmodified tool-native export showing prompts, tool calls, file modifications, and key milestones. Never synthesize, rewrite, trim, or repair it. If it is missing, too large, incomplete, or affected by a crashed tool, state that plainly and follow the course rule to contact the instructor before submission when necessary.

Run the deterministic checks:

```bash
python scripts/preflight_submission.py \
  path/to/report.pdf \
  --session path/to/session.json \
  --student-prefix student_or_team \
  --assignment a01
```

Then manually complete the evidence checklist because no script can prove that references, reasoning, or personal verification are genuine. Do not call the submission ready while a Gate 0 risk remains.

# Association Rules for Online Retail Baskets

**Student:** Raimova Alina  
**Team:** Individual  
**Email:** aaraimova@edu.hse.ru  
**Date:** 2026-10-06  
**Assignment:** HW4, Association Rules (Week 4)

## Abstract

This study asks whether products bought on the same invoice reveal useful retail association rules. It builds 17,080 invoice baskets from the UCI Online Retail data, implements FP-Growth in a browser app, and uses a notebook to compare Apriori, thresholds, and time periods. At 2% minimum support and 30% minimum confidence, 96 rules remain, all with lift above 1. A teacup rule is worth testing as a cross-sell recommendation, but historical co-purchases alone cannot establish that the recommendation will increase sales.

**Index Terms —** association rules, market basket analysis, FP-Growth, Apriori, cross-sell

## 1. Introduction

### Problem statement and motivation

The task is to turn retail invoice lines into baskets and find products bought together more often than expected. Each `InvoiceNo` is one transaction; `StockCode` identifies a product and `Description` labels it. The app reports support, confidence, and lift so that a co-purchase count is not mistaken for evidence that a promotion will work.

### Concrete example and contributions

In the cleaned data, 541 of 17,080 invoices contain both green and roses Regency teacups. The question is whether this pattern is common and strong enough to investigate, and whether it persists later.

This work (1) implements a working invoice-basket FP-Growth and rule display with 11 passing self-checks and (2) compares mining methods and rule choices using the executed analysis notebook. The notebook is an analysis artifact; the browser app runs from `index.html`, `script.js`, `style.css`, and `transactions.js` without Python.

## 2. Related Work

The UCI Online Retail record defines the source fields and notes that many customers are wholesalers [1]. Agrawal and Srikant describe Apriori's frequent-itemset search and rule generation [2]. Han, Pei, and Yin introduce FP-Growth, which grows patterns from an FP-tree rather than generating Apriori candidates [3]. Kohavi, Henne, and Sommerfield explain why a randomized controlled experiment is needed to estimate the effect of a proposed online feature [4].

### Alternatives considered

Apriori is a clear baseline, using candidate generation and downward-closure pruning. FP-Growth is the chosen browser miner; the notebook compares its output with Apriori rather than assuming it is always faster. A rule selected only by confidence was rejected as a decision method because confidence ignores how common the consequent already is.

## 3. Method

### Pipeline and decisions

1. Start with the 541,909-row UCI workbook [1]. Exclude cancellations and adjustments, nonpositive quantity or price, blank descriptions or customer IDs, and nonproduct codes; normalize stock codes and product labels as described in `readme.md`.
2. Group by `InvoiceNo`, deduplicate each `StockCode` within an invoice, and exclude baskets with fewer than two distinct items. The resulting conceptual invoice–item matrix has **17,080 rows**, **3,653 product columns**, and **384,911 present invoice–item cells**. Its data are stored compactly in `transactions.js`.
3. Mine frequent itemsets and generate both directions of each rule. For antecedent \(A\), consequent \(B\), and \(N\) baskets, compute

   \[
   \operatorname{support}=\frac{\operatorname{count}(A\cup B)}{N},\qquad
   \operatorname{confidence}=\frac{\operatorname{count}(A\cup B)}{\operatorname{count}(A)},\qquad
   \operatorname{lift}=\frac{\operatorname{confidence}}{\operatorname{count}(B)/N}.
   \]

   Undefined denominators are handled explicitly. At the chosen setting, retain rules with support at least **2%** (at least **342** invoices), confidence at least **30%**, and lift **greater than 1**.
4. For a historical check, reconstruct dated baskets from the original workbook's `InvoiceDate`, apply the same cleaning, and compare January–August 2011 with September–November 2011. December 2010 and incomplete December 2011 are excluded from this comparison. The exported app baskets do not contain dates; no dates were simulated.

### Tools and configuration

The browser implementation is plain JavaScript with no build step. The analysis notebook used Python **3.13.7** [5], pandas **3.0.3** [6], and openpyxl **3.1.5** [7] on Darwin; the CPU and total RAM were not recorded. Apriori uses posting-set intersections and downward-closure pruning; FP-Growth uses an FP-tree and conditional paths. Both analyze the same already loaded baskets. The code has deterministic tie ordering and no random seed; benchmark order alternates across five timing repeats. The notebook's 1% benchmark uses a minimum of 171 baskets, times only the mining functions, and measures traced Python allocation in separate runs.

## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Frequent-itemset benchmark

**Table 1 — Same baskets and 1% support, from the executed notebook.** Time is the median of five runs; memory is peak `tracemalloc` allocation in a separate run, not total process memory.

| Algorithm | Frequent itemsets | Median mining time | Peak traced allocation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Apriori | 1,219 | 1.899 s | 28.6 MiB |
| FP-Growth | 1,219 | 1.103 s | 59.5 MiB |

The itemsets and their counts matched exactly. FP-Growth was faster in this run, while Apriori used less traced memory; this compares these two Python implementations on this machine, not the algorithms in every setting.

### 4.2 Threshold research and trade-off

The notebook first mined at 0.5% support, yielding 5,255 itemsets and 21,026 possible directed rules. Its support and confidence histograms show that 20,918 candidate rules have support below 2% and 10,303 have confidence below 30%. The 2%/30% choice leaves a manageable 96 rules with at least 342 joint invoices per rule. It is a practical screening choice, not an optimal threshold proved for every business goal.

**Table 2 — Threshold sweep, from the executed notebook.** All listed rules also had lift above 1.

| Minimum support | Minimum confidence | Frequent itemsets | Rules |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.5% | 30% | 5,255 | 10,723 |
| 1% | 30% | 1,219 | 950 |
| 2% | 30% | 294 | 96 |
| 3% | 30% | 115 | 12 |
| 2% | 10% | 294 | 108 |
| 2% | 40% | 294 | 76 |
| 2% | 60% | 294 | 20 |

Raising support removes rare itemsets and their possible rules because a superset cannot be more frequent than its subsets. Raising confidence leaves the frequent itemsets unchanged but removes rule directions with weaker conditional probabilities. Lower thresholds offer more possible discoveries and more noise to inspect; higher thresholds are easier to review but can hide useful niche combinations. At 2% support, the notebook also found 108 rules at 20% confidence, 45 at 2.5% support with 30% confidence, and 275 at 1.5% support with 30% confidence.

### 4.3 Useful versus misleading rules

**Table 3 — Single-product rules across all 17,080 cleaned invoices.** Counts for \(A\), \(B\), and both are baskets containing those items, not units sold.

| Judgment and rule | count(A) | count(B) | count(A∪B) | Support | Confidence | Lift |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Investigate:** GREEN REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER [22697] → ROSES REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER [22699] | 691 | 780 | 541 | 3.17% | 78.29% | 17.14 |
| **Reject:** ALARM CLOCK BAKELIKE RED [22727] → WHITE HANGING HEART T-LIGHT HOLDER [85123A] | 877 | 1,959 | 98 | 0.57% | 11.17% | 0.97 |

The teacup rule has a substantial antecedent count, 541 co-purchases, and lift far above 1. A recommendation for the roses teacup when a shopper selects the green teacup is worth investigating. The weak alarm-clock rule has 98 co-purchases, which might look meaningful as a raw count, but the holder appears in **11.47%** of all baskets even without the clock; its **11.17%** confidence is slightly *below* that baseline. It fails the chosen support and confidence thresholds and lift > 1, so it should not drive a cross-sell. In this dataset the most frequent single item appears in only 11.47% of baskets; there is no very-high-confidence, near-unit-lift example among the chosen high-confidence rules.

**Verification worksheet:** the teacup figures follow from \(541/17{,}080=3.1674\%\), \(541/691=78.2923\%\), and \((541/691)/(780/17{,}080)=17.1440\). The app's self-checks passed **11/11**, and direct app counts matched these three inputs; this worksheet was prepared with AI assistance and still needs the student's own check before submission.

### 4.4 Rule direction

For **JUMBO BAG PINK POLKADOT [22386] → JUMBO BAG RED RETROSPOT [85099B]**, 546 invoices contain both, out of 869 with the pink bag: confidence is **62.83%**. In reverse, the same 546 are divided by 1,584 invoices with the red bag: confidence is **34.47%**. Support is **3.20%** and lift is **6.77** in either direction. Confidence differs because the antecedent denominator changes; joint count, support, and lift do not.

### 4.5 Validation before action

The teacup rule was chosen from the full dataset before the date check. The notebook reconstructed dates from the original UCI workbook and confirmed that the rebuilt baskets exactly match the app's basket multiset. **Table 4** uses full months only and leaves out 1,981 invoices from December 2010 and December 2011.

| Period | Baskets | Green A | Roses B | Both | Support | Confidence | Lift |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan–Aug 2011 | 9,220 | 448 | 506 | 360 | 3.90% | 80.36% | 14.64 |
| Sep–Nov 2011 | 5,879 | 192 | 218 | 144 | 2.45% | 75.00% | 20.23 |

The later period has 144 joint invoices and passes the chosen support, confidence, and lift filters. Confidence fell **5.36 percentage points**; an approximate 95% interval for that change is **−12.50 to +1.79 points**, so a decline larger than 10 points cannot be ruled out. November alone had only **1.70% support**, below the 2% cutoff. This is evidence of an aggregate association later in the historical record, with a clear monthly weakness. Because the rule was selected using the full data, this split is retrospective validation rather than an independent held-out discovery test. The notebook also tried other products: pink → red jumbo bags changed from 63.35% to 62.32% confidence; red → green alarm clocks rose from 48.77% to 72.24%, showing that other rules can drift. These additional checks are exploratory, not reasons to replace the preselected rule after seeing the outcomes.

**Controlled cross-sell proposal:** Among shoppers who add the green teacup while the roses teacup is absent, assign customers 50/50 to a fixed control or treatment group. Control shows the current item in the existing recommendation slot; treatment shows the roses teacup in that same slot, with the same prices and promotions. The primary metric is the roses-teacup purchase rate per eligible checkout; guardrails are gross margin per eligible checkout, green-teacup checkout completion, and returns. Estimate the eligible-session baseline in a pilot, then set a sample size for 80% power against a prespecified, commercially meaningful lift; evaluate the full planned run with a 95% confidence interval. Deploy only if the incremental attach-rate interval is above zero and guardrails show no material harm. **No live experiment was run.** The observed 75% basket confidence is not a control-group attach-rate estimate because the data do not record when an item was added to a cart.

## 5. Discussion

### Association is not causation

Lift **17.14** says the two teacups co-occurred about 17 times as often as an independence calculation predicts; it does **not** predict a 17-fold sales increase. Wholesalers may intentionally buy matching color variants, or the products may share displays or promotions. Such factors can produce high lift without any effect from recommending one product. Only the proposed randomized intervention can estimate incremental sales from the recommendation [4].

### Data issue, resolution, and limits

During the date reconstruction, **30 `InvoiceNo` values had more than one raw `InvoiceDate`**, at most one minute apart. Therefore, a one-timestamp-per-invoice assumption did not hold. The notebook assigned the earliest timestamp to each invoice, verified that each affected invoice stayed within one month, and confirmed an exact match of the rebuilt basket multiset to the app data. This resolves the split assignment for these periods but does not create timestamps in the exported app data.

The time benchmark favored FP-Growth, while its traced allocation was larger. The rule-screening choice reduced 950 rules at 1%/30% to 96 at 2%/30%, yet November showed that a useful aggregate rule can dip below the threshold. A next improvement is a genuinely prospective test: select a rule using data available at one cutoff, evaluate it on invoices collected strictly afterward, then run the controlled cross-sell if it still passes prespecified checks.

## 6. My comments

**Student review required:** In your own words, state what surprised you, whether you agree with the teacup interpretation, one alternative you considered, and one result you personally checked. The arithmetic in §4.3 is a ready-to-check example; do not claim you checked it until you have done so.

## 7. AI Usage Disclosure

### AI tools used and how they were used

Codex assisted with the browser-app implementation, analysis-notebook code, debugging, experiment interpretation, reference checking, and this report draft. **Student review required:** confirm the exact AI tools and versions against the authentic session export before submission.

### What I personally verified

**Student review required:** Record only checks you actually performed yourself, for example recalculating the teacup metrics from the counts in Table 3 or rerunning the notebook and comparing Table 1.

### What I trusted without verification

**Student review required:** State which, if any, AI-assisted outputs you did not independently verify. The current draft does not attribute any personal verification to the student.

### Session log

An authentic, unmodified tool-native `session.json` export has **not been attached to this draft**. Add it only from the actual tool export; do not reconstruct it from this report.

## References

[1] D. Chen, “Online Retail,” *UCI Machine Learning Repository*, 2015, doi: 10.24432/C5BW33. [Online]. Available: [https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/352/online+retail](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/352/online+retail). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.

[2] R. Agrawal and R. Srikant, “Fast Algorithms for Mining Association Rules in Large Databases,” in *Proc. 20th Int. Conf. Very Large Data Bases*, 1994, pp. 487–499. [Online]. Available: [https://www.vldb.org/conf/1994/P487.PDF](https://www.vldb.org/conf/1994/P487.PDF). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.

[3] J. Han, J. Pei, and Y. Yin, “Mining Frequent Patterns without Candidate Generation,” in *Proc. ACM SIGMOD Int. Conf. Management of Data*, 2000. [Online]. Available: [https://sigmodrecord.org/publications/sigmodRecord/0006/pdfs/Mining%20Frequent%20Patterns%20without%20Candidate%20Generation.pdf](https://sigmodrecord.org/publications/sigmodRecord/0006/pdfs/Mining%20Frequent%20Patterns%20without%20Candidate%20Generation.pdf). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.

[4] R. Kohavi, R. M. Henne, and D. Sommerfield, “Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HiPPO,” in *Proc. 13th ACM SIGKDD Int. Conf. Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining*, 2007. [Online]. Available: [https://ai.stanford.edu/~ronnyk/GuideControlledExperiments.pdf](https://ai.stanford.edu/~ronnyk/GuideControlledExperiments.pdf). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.

[5] Python Software Foundation, “Python 3.13 Documentation.” [Online]. Available: [https://docs.python.org/3.13/](https://docs.python.org/3.13/). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.

[6] pandas development team, “pandas Documentation.” [Online]. Available: [https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.

# Association Rules for Online Retail Baskets

**Student:** Raimova Alina  
**Team:** Individual  
**Email:** aaraimova@edu.hse.ru  
**Date:** 2026-10-06  
**Assignment:** HW4, Association Rules (Week 4)

## Abstract

This study asks whether products bought on the same invoice reveal useful retail association rules. It builds 17,080 invoice baskets from the UCI Online Retail data, implements FP-Growth in a browser app, and uses a notebook to compare Apriori, thresholds, and time periods. At 2% minimum support and 30% minimum confidence, 96 rules remain, all with lift above 1. A teacup rule is worth testing as a cross-sell recommendation, but historical co-purchases alone cannot establish that the recommendation will increase sales.

**Index Terms —** association rules, market basket analysis, FP-Growth, Apriori, cross-sell

## 1. Introduction

### Problem statement and motivation

The task is to turn retail invoice lines into baskets and find products bought together more often than expected. Each `InvoiceNo` is one transaction; `StockCode` identifies a product and `Description` labels it. The app reports support, confidence, and lift so that a co-purchase count is not mistaken for evidence that a promotion will work.

### Concrete example and contributions

In the cleaned data, 541 of 17,080 invoices contain both green and roses Regency teacups. The question is whether this pattern is common and strong enough to investigate, and whether it persists later.

This work (1) implements a working invoice-basket FP-Growth and rule display with 11 passing self-checks and (2) compares mining methods and rule choices using the executed analysis notebook. The notebook is an analysis artifact; the browser app runs from `index.html`, `script.js`, `style.css`, and `transactions.js` without Python.

## 2. Related Work

The UCI Online Retail record defines the source fields and notes that many customers are wholesalers [1]. Agrawal and Srikant describe Apriori's frequent-itemset search and rule generation [2]. Han, Pei, and Yin introduce FP-Growth, which grows patterns from an FP-tree rather than generating Apriori candidates [3]. Kohavi, Henne, and Sommerfield explain why a randomized controlled experiment is needed to estimate the effect of a proposed online feature [4].

### Alternatives considered

Apriori is a clear baseline, using candidate generation and downward-closure pruning. FP-Growth is the chosen browser miner; the notebook compares its output with Apriori rather than assuming it is always faster. A rule selected only by confidence was rejected as a decision method because confidence ignores how common the consequent already is.

## 3. Method

### Pipeline and decisions

1. Start with the 541,909-row UCI workbook [1]. Exclude cancellations and adjustments, nonpositive quantity or price, blank descriptions or customer IDs, and nonproduct codes; normalize stock codes and product labels as described in `readme.md`.
2. Group by `InvoiceNo`, deduplicate each `StockCode` within an invoice, and exclude baskets with fewer than two distinct items. The resulting conceptual invoice–item matrix has **17,080 rows**, **3,653 product columns**, and **384,911 present invoice–item cells**. Its data are stored compactly in `transactions.js`.
3. Mine frequent itemsets and generate both directions of each rule. For antecedent \(A\), consequent \(B\), and \(N\) baskets, compute

   \[
   \operatorname{support}=\frac{\operatorname{count}(A\cup B)}{N},\qquad
   \operatorname{confidence}=\frac{\operatorname{count}(A\cup B)}{\operatorname{count}(A)},\qquad
   \operatorname{lift}=\frac{\operatorname{confidence}}{\operatorname{count}(B)/N}.
   \]

   Undefined denominators are handled explicitly. At the chosen setting, retain rules with support at least **2%** (at least **342** invoices), confidence at least **30%**, and lift **greater than 1**.
4. For a historical check, reconstruct dated baskets from the original workbook's `InvoiceDate`, apply the same cleaning, and compare January–August 2011 with September–November 2011. December 2010 and incomplete December 2011 are excluded from this comparison. The exported app baskets do not contain dates; no dates were simulated.

### Tools and configuration

The browser implementation is plain JavaScript with no build step. The analysis notebook used Python **3.13.7** [5], pandas **3.0.3** [6], and openpyxl **3.1.5** [7] on Darwin; the CPU and total RAM were not recorded. Apriori uses posting-set intersections and downward-closure pruning; FP-Growth uses an FP-tree and conditional paths. Both analyze the same already loaded baskets. The code has deterministic tie ordering and no random seed; benchmark order alternates across five timing repeats. The notebook's 1% benchmark uses a minimum of 171 baskets, times only the mining functions, and measures traced Python allocation in separate runs.

## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Frequent-itemset benchmark

**Table 1 — Same baskets and 1% support, from the executed notebook.** Time is the median of five runs; memory is peak `tracemalloc` allocation in a separate run, not total process memory.

| Algorithm | Frequent itemsets | Median mining time | Peak traced allocation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Apriori | 1,219 | 1.899 s | 28.6 MiB |
| FP-Growth | 1,219 | 1.103 s | 59.5 MiB |

The itemsets and their counts matched exactly. FP-Growth was faster in this run, while Apriori used less traced memory; this compares these two Python implementations on this machine, not the algorithms in every setting.

### 4.2 Threshold research and trade-off

The notebook first mined at 0.5% support, yielding 5,255 itemsets and 21,026 possible directed rules. Its support and confidence histograms show that 20,918 candidate rules have support below 2% and 10,303 have confidence below 30%. The 2%/30% choice leaves a manageable 96 rules with at least 342 joint invoices per rule. It is a practical screening choice, not an optimal threshold proved for every business goal.

**Table 2 — Threshold sweep, from the executed notebook.** All listed rules also had lift above 1.

| Minimum support | Minimum confidence | Frequent itemsets | Rules |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.5% | 30% | 5,255 | 10,723 |
| 1% | 30% | 1,219 | 950 |
| 2% | 30% | 294 | 96 |
| 3% | 30% | 115 | 12 |
| 2% | 10% | 294 | 108 |
| 2% | 40% | 294 | 76 |
| 2% | 60% | 294 | 20 |

Raising support removes rare itemsets and their possible rules because a superset cannot be more frequent than its subsets. Raising confidence leaves the frequent itemsets unchanged but removes rule directions with weaker conditional probabilities. Lower thresholds offer more possible discoveries and more noise to inspect; higher thresholds are easier to review but can hide useful niche combinations. At 2% support, the notebook also found 108 rules at 20% confidence, 45 at 2.5% support with 30% confidence, and 275 at 1.5% support with 30% confidence.

### 4.3 Useful versus misleading rules

**Table 3 — Single-product rules across all 17,080 cleaned invoices.** Counts for \(A\), \(B\), and both are baskets containing those items, not units sold.

| Judgment and rule | count(A) | count(B) | count(A∪B) | Support | Confidence | Lift |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Investigate:** GREEN REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER [22697] → ROSES REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER [22699] | 691 | 780 | 541 | 3.17% | 78.29% | 17.14 |
| **Reject:** ALARM CLOCK BAKELIKE RED [22727] → WHITE HANGING HEART T-LIGHT HOLDER [85123A] | 877 | 1,959 | 98 | 0.57% | 11.17% | 0.97 |

The teacup rule has a substantial antecedent count, 541 co-purchases, and lift far above 1. A recommendation for the roses teacup when a shopper selects the green teacup is worth investigating. The weak alarm-clock rule has 98 co-purchases, which might look meaningful as a raw count, but the holder appears in **11.47%** of all baskets even without the clock; its **11.17%** confidence is slightly *below* that baseline. It fails the chosen support and confidence thresholds and lift > 1, so it should not drive a cross-sell. In this dataset the most frequent single item appears in only 11.47% of baskets; there is no very-high-confidence, near-unit-lift example among the chosen high-confidence rules.

**Verification worksheet:** the teacup figures follow from \(541/17{,}080=3.1674\%\), \(541/691=78.2923\%\), and \((541/691)/(780/17{,}080)=17.1440\). The app's self-checks passed **11/11**, and direct app counts matched these three inputs; this worksheet was prepared with AI assistance and still needs the student's own check before submission.

### 4.4 Rule direction

For **JUMBO BAG PINK POLKADOT [22386] → JUMBO BAG RED RETROSPOT [85099B]**, 546 invoices contain both, out of 869 with the pink bag: confidence is **62.83%**. In reverse, the same 546 are divided by 1,584 invoices with the red bag: confidence is **34.47%**. Support is **3.20%** and lift is **6.77** in either direction. Confidence differs because the antecedent denominator changes; joint count, support, and lift do not.

### 4.5 Validation before action

The teacup rule was chosen from the full dataset before the date check. The notebook reconstructed dates from the original UCI workbook and confirmed that the rebuilt baskets exactly match the app's basket multiset. **Table 4** uses full months only and leaves out 1,981 invoices from December 2010 and December 2011.

| Period | Baskets | Green A | Roses B | Both | Support | Confidence | Lift |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan–Aug 2011 | 9,220 | 448 | 506 | 360 | 3.90% | 80.36% | 14.64 |
| Sep–Nov 2011 | 5,879 | 192 | 218 | 144 | 2.45% | 75.00% | 20.23 |

The later period has 144 joint invoices and passes the chosen support, confidence, and lift filters. Confidence fell **5.36 percentage points**; an approximate 95% interval for that change is **−12.50 to +1.79 points**, so a decline larger than 10 points cannot be ruled out. November alone had only **1.70% support**, below the 2% cutoff. This is evidence of an aggregate association later in the historical record, with a clear monthly weakness. Because the rule was selected using the full data, this split is retrospective validation rather than an independent held-out discovery test. The notebook also tried other products: pink → red jumbo bags changed from 63.35% to 62.32% confidence; red → green alarm clocks rose from 48.77% to 72.24%, showing that other rules can drift. These additional checks are exploratory, not reasons to replace the preselected rule after seeing the outcomes.

**Controlled cross-sell proposal:** Among shoppers who add the green teacup while the roses teacup is absent, assign customers 50/50 to a fixed control or treatment group. Control shows the current item in the existing recommendation slot; treatment shows the roses teacup in that same slot, with the same prices and promotions. The primary metric is the roses-teacup purchase rate per eligible checkout; guardrails are gross margin per eligible checkout, green-teacup checkout completion, and returns. Estimate the eligible-session baseline in a pilot, then set a sample size for 80% power against a prespecified, commercially meaningful lift; evaluate the full planned run with a 95% confidence interval. Deploy only if the incremental attach-rate interval is above zero and guardrails show no material harm. **No live experiment was run.** The observed 75% basket confidence is not a control-group attach-rate estimate because the data do not record when an item was added to a cart.

## 5. Discussion

### Association is not causation

Lift **17.14** says the two teacups co-occurred about 17 times as often as an independence calculation predicts; it does **not** predict a 17-fold sales increase. Wholesalers may intentionally buy matching color variants, or the products may share displays or promotions. Such factors can produce high lift without any effect from recommending one product. Only the proposed randomized intervention can estimate incremental sales from the recommendation [4].

### Data issue, resolution, and limits

During the date reconstruction, **30 `InvoiceNo` values had more than one raw `InvoiceDate`**, at most one minute apart. Therefore, a one-timestamp-per-invoice assumption did not hold. The notebook assigned the earliest timestamp to each invoice, verified that each affected invoice stayed within one month, and confirmed an exact match of the rebuilt basket multiset to the app data. This resolves the split assignment for these periods but does not create timestamps in the exported app data.

The time benchmark favored FP-Growth, while its traced allocation was larger. The rule-screening choice reduced 950 rules at 1%/30% to 96 at 2%/30%, yet November showed that a useful aggregate rule can dip below the threshold. A next improvement is a genuinely prospective test: select a rule using data available at one cutoff, evaluate it on invoices collected strictly afterward, then run the controlled cross-sell if it still passes prespecified checks.

## 6. My comments

**Student review required:** In your own words, state what surprised you, whether you agree with the teacup interpretation, one alternative you considered, and one result you personally checked. The arithmetic in §4.3 is a ready-to-check example; do not claim you checked it until you have done so.

## 7. AI Usage Disclosure

Codex assisted with the browser-app implementation, analysis-notebook code, debugging, experiment interpretation, reference checking, and this report draft. **Student review required:** confirm the exact AI tools and versions against the authentic session export before submission.

### What I trusted without verification

**Student review required:** State which, if any, AI-assisted outputs you did not independently verify. The current draft does not attribute any personal verification to the student.

An authentic, unmodified tool-native `session.json` export has **not been attached to this draft**. Add it only from the actual tool export; do not reconstruct it from this report.

## Establish the assignment

If the weekly specification is missing, do not invent the task. You may inspect the repository and prepare a plan, but ask for the specification before implementing a supposedly final solution.

## Meet the grading contract

Each assignment is graded on two binary criteria:

- **c1 - Understanding:** identify the problem correctly and cite valid, accurately attributed references.
- **c2 - AI Management:** deliver a working solution, accurate reasoning, and verifiable evidence of checking the AI-assisted work.

A major failure triggers Gate 0 and a score of zero. Treat an invalid or hallucinated citation, fabricated benchmark, claim-evidence mismatch, nonexistent API, solution claimed to work when it does not, unsupported root cause, cherry-picked result, or verification claimed without being performed as a submission blocker. A clean c2 requires all three: the solution runs, the reasoning is accurate, and at least one critical output is personally verified and described.

## Run the Top-Down 5-Loop

Keep an evidence ledger throughout the work: each important claim should point to a command output, code location, generated table or figure, hand calculation, or checked source.

1. **BUILD** - Inspect existing work first, then implement the smallest working baseline. Record the environment, dependency versions, data split, seed, configuration, and exact commands. Run the code; a plausible-looking implementation is not evidence.
2. **ASK WHY** - State the assumptions, identify 1-3 realistic alternatives, and explain the chosen tradeoff without claiming one method is universally best. Flag conclusions that require the student's own judgment and ask the student to confirm or rewrite them in their own words.
3. **TEST** - Run relevant tests and sanity checks. Prepare at least one transparent manual verification, such as a metric on one example, a small derivation, or a line-by-line comparison with raw output. Do not claim the student performed it until the student confirms that they did.
4. **EXPLAIN** - Draft a concise technical explanation grounded in the evidence ledger. Preserve the student's voice: ask for their interpretation of the result and revise the discussion around it. If their input is unavailable, label the passage as a draft requiring personal review.
5. **IMPROVE** - Change one justified variable, rerun the same evaluation, and compare against the baseline. Record negative or unchanged results honestly.

Do not hide failures. Preserve one real failure with its symptom, root cause, fix, and verification. If no meaningful failure occurred, do not invent one; describe a real limitation or obtain a reproducible failure case through a safe, relevant test.

{"i":2,"result":{"status":"fulfilled","value":{"chunk_id":"c7ad8c","wall_time_seconds":0.130840042,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":4098,"output":"# Association Rules for Online Retail Baskets

**Student:** Raimova Alina  
**Team:** Individual  
**Email:** aaraimova@edu.hse.ru  
**Date:** 2026-10-06  
**Assignment:** HW4, Association Rules (Week 4)

## Abstract

This study asks whether products bought on the same invoice reveal useful retail association rules. It builds 17,080 invoice baskets from the UCI Online Retail data, implements FP-Growth in a browser app, and uses a notebook to compare Apriori, thresholds, and time periods. At 2% minimum support and 30% minimum confidence, 96 rules remain, all with lift above 1. A teacup rule is worth testing as a cross-sell recommendation, but historical co-purchases alone cannot establish that the recommendation will increase sales.

**Index Terms —** association rules, market basket analysis, FP-Growth, Apriori, cross-sell

## 1. Introduction

### Problem statement and motivation

The task is to turn retail invoice lines into baskets and find products bought together more often than expected. Each `InvoiceNo` is one transaction; `StockCode` identifies a product and `Description` labels it. The app reports support, confidence, and lift so that a co-purchase count is not mistaken for evidence that a promotion will work.

### Concrete example and contributions

In the cleaned data, 541 of 17,080 invoices contain both green and roses Regency teacups. The question is whether this pattern is common and strong enough to investigate, and whether it persists later.

This work (1) implements a working invoice-basket FP-Growth and rule display with 11 passing self-checks and (2) compares mining methods and rule choices using the executed analysis notebook. The notebook is an analysis artifact; the browser app runs from `index.html`, `script.js`, `style.css`, and `transactions.js` without Python.

## 2. Related Work

The UCI Online Retail record defines the source fields and notes that many customers are wholesalers [1]. Agrawal and Srikant describe Apriori's frequent-itemset search and rule generation [2]. Han, Pei, and Yin introduce FP-Growth, which grows patterns from an FP-tree rather than generating Apriori candidates [3]. Kohavi, Henne, and Sommerfield explain why a randomized controlled experiment is needed to estimate the effect of a proposed online feature [4].

### Alternatives considered

Apriori is a clear baseline, using candidate generation and downward-closure pruning. FP-Growth is the chosen browser miner; the notebook compares its output with Apriori rather than assuming it is always faster. A rule selected only by confidence was rejected as a decision method because confidence ignores how common the consequent already is.

## 3. Method

### Pipeline and decisions

1. Start with the 541,909-row UCI workbook [1]. Exclude cancellations and adjustments, nonpositive quantity or price, blank descriptions or customer IDs, and nonproduct codes; normalize stock codes and product labels as described in `readme.md`.
2. Group by `InvoiceNo`, deduplicate each `StockCode` within an invoice, and exclude baskets with fewer than two distinct items. The resulting conceptual invoice–item matrix has **17,080 rows**, **3,653 product columns**, and **384,911 present invoice–item cells**. Its data are stored compactly in `transactions.js`.
3. Mine frequent itemsets and generate both directions of each rule. For antecedent \(A\), consequent \(B\), and \(N\) baskets, compute

   \[
   \operatorname{support}=\frac{\operatorname{count}(A\cup B)}{N},\qquad
   \operatorname{confidence}=\frac{\operatorname{count}(A\cup B)}{\operatorname{count}(A)},\qquad
   \operatorname{lift}=\frac{\operatorname{confidence}}{\operatorname{count}(B)/N}.
   \]

   Undefined denominators are handled explicitly. At the chosen setting, retain rules with support at least **2%** (at least **342** invoices), confidence at least **30%**, and lift **greater than 1**.
4. For a historical check, reconstruct dated baskets from the original workbook's `InvoiceDate`, apply the same cleaning, and compare January–August 2011 with September–November 2011. December 2010 and incomplete December 2011 are excluded from this comparison. The exported app baskets do not contain dates; no dates were simulated.

### Tools and configuration

The browser implementation is plain JavaScript with no build step. The analysis notebook used Python **3.13.7** [5], pandas **3.0.3** [6], and openpyxl **3.1.5** [7] on Darwin; the CPU and total RAM were not recorded. Apriori uses posting-set intersections and downward-closure pruning; FP-Growth uses an FP-tree and conditional paths. Both analyze the same already loaded baskets. The code has deterministic tie ordering and no random seed; benchmark order alternates across five timing repeats. The notebook's 1% benchmark uses a minimum of 171 baskets, times only the mining functions, and measures traced Python allocation in separate runs.

## 4. Experiments

### 4.1 Frequent-itemset benchmark

**Table 1 — Same baskets and 1% support, from the executed notebook.** Time is the median of five runs; memory is peak `tracemalloc` allocation in a separate run, not total process memory.

| Algorithm | Frequent itemsets | Median mining time | Peak traced allocation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Apriori | 1,219 | 1.899 s | 28.6 MiB |
| FP-Growth | 1,219 | 1.103 s | 59.5 MiB |

The itemsets and their counts matched exactly. FP-Growth was faster in this run, while Apriori used less traced memory; this compares these two Python implementations on this machine, not the algorithms in every setting.

### 4.2 Threshold research and trade-off

The notebook first mined at 0.5% support, yielding 5,255 itemsets and 21,026 possible directed rules. Its support and confidence histograms show that 20,918 candidate rules have support below 2% and 10,303 have confidence below 30%. The 2%/30% choice leaves a manageable 96 rules with at least 342 joint invoices per rule. It is a practical screening choice, not an optimal threshold proved for every business goal.

**Table 2 — Threshold sweep, from the executed notebook.** All listed rules also had lift above 1.

| Minimum support | Minimum confidence | Frequent itemsets | Rules |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.5% | 30% | 5,255 | 10,723 |
| 1% | 30% | 1,219 | 950 |
| 2% | 30% | 294 | 96 |
| 3% | 30% | 115 | 12 |
| 2% | 10% | 294 | 108 |
| 2% | 40% | 294 | 76 |
| 2% | 60% | 294 | 20 |

Raising support removes rare itemsets and their possible rules because a superset cannot be more frequent than its subsets. Raising confidence leaves the frequent itemsets unchanged but removes rule directions with weaker conditional probabilities. Lower thresholds offer more possible discoveries and more noise to inspect; higher thresholds are easier to review but can hide useful niche combinations. At 2% support, the notebook also found 108 rules at 20% confidence, 45 at 2.5% support with 30% confidence, and 275 at 1.5% support with 30% confidence.

### 4.3 Useful versus misleading rules

**Table 3 — Single-product rules across all 17,080 cleaned invoices.** Counts for \(A\), \(B\), and both are baskets containing those items, not units sold.

| Judgment and rule | count(A) | count(B) | count(A∪B) | Support | Confidence | Lift |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Investigate:** GREEN REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER [22697] → ROSES REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER [22699] | 691 | 780 | 541 | 3.17% | 78.29% | 17.14 |
| **Reject:** ALARM CLOCK BAKELIKE RED [22727] → WHITE HANGING HEART T-LIGHT HOLDER [85123A] | 877 | 1,959 | 98 | 0.57% | 11.17% | 0.97 |

The teacup rule has a substantial antecedent count, 541 co-purchases, and lift far above 1. A recommendation for the roses teacup when a shopper selects the green teacup is worth investigating. The weak alarm-clock rule has 98 co-purchases, which might look meaningful as a raw count, but the holder appears in **11.47%** of all baskets even without the clock; its **11.17%** confidence is slightly *below* that baseline. It fails the chosen support and confidence thresholds and lift > 1, so it should not drive a cross-sell. In this dataset the most frequent single item appears in only 11.47% of baskets; there is no very-high-confidence, near-unit-lift example among the chosen high-confidence rules.

**Verification worksheet:** the teacup figures follow from \(541/17{,}080=3.1674\%\), \(541/691=78.2923\%\), and \((541/691)/(780/17{,}080)=17.1440\). The app's self-checks passed **11/11**, and direct app counts matched these three inputs; this worksheet was prepared with AI assistance and still needs the student's own check before submission.

### 4.4 Rule direction

For **JUMBO BAG PINK POLKADOT [22386] → JUMBO BAG RED RETROSPOT [85099B]**, 546 invoices contain both, out of 869 with the pink bag: confidence is **62.83%**. In reverse, the same 546 are divided by 1,584 invoices with the red bag: confidence is **34.47%**. Support is **3.20%** and lift is **6.77** in either direction. Confidence differs because the antecedent denominator changes; joint count, support, and lift do not.

### 4.5 Validation before action

The teacup rule was chosen from the full dataset before the date check. The notebook reconstructed dates from the original UCI workbook and confirmed that the rebuilt baskets exactly match the app's basket multiset. **Table 4** uses full months only and leaves out 1,981 invoices from December 2010 and December 2011.

| Period | Baskets | Green A | Roses B | Both | Support | Confidence | Lift |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan–Aug 2011 | 9,220 | 448 | 506 | 360 | 3.90% | 80.36% | 14.64 |
| Sep–Nov 2011 | 5,879 | 192 | 218 | 144 | 2.45% | 75.00% | 20.23 |

The later period has 144 joint invoices and passes the chosen support, confidence, and lift filters. Confidence fell **5.36 percentage points**; an approximate 95% interval for that change is **−12.50 to +1.79 points**, so a decline larger than 10 points cannot be ruled out. November alone had only **1.70% support**, below the 2% cutoff. This is evidence of an aggregate association later in the historical record, with a clear monthly weakness. Because the rule was selected using the full data, this split is retrospective validation rather than an independent held-out discovery test. The notebook also tried other products: pink → red jumbo bags changed from 63.35% to 62.32% confidence; red → green alarm clocks rose from 48.77% to 72.24%, showing that other rules can drift. These additional checks are exploratory, not reasons to replace the preselected rule after seeing the outcomes.

**Controlled cross-sell proposal:** Among shoppers who add the green teacup while the roses teacup is absent, assign customers 50/50 to a fixed control or treatment group. Control shows the current item in the existing recommendation slot; treatment shows the roses teacup in that same slot, with the same prices and promotions. The primary metric is the roses-teacup purchase rate per eligible checkout; guardrails are gross margin per eligible checkout, green-teacup checkout completion, and returns. Estimate the eligible-session baseline in a pilot, then set a sample size for 80% power against a prespecified, commercially meaningful lift; evaluate the full planned run with a 95% confidence interval. Deploy only if the incremental attach-rate interval is above zero and guardrails show no material harm. **No live experiment was run.** The observed 75% basket confidence is not a control-group attach-rate estimate because the data do not record when an item was added to a cart.

## 5. Discussion

### Association is not causation

Lift **17.14** says the two teacups co-occurred about 17 times as often as an independence calculation predicts; it does **not** predict a 17-fold sales increase. Wholesalers may intentionally buy matching color variants, or the products may share displays or promotions. Such factors can produce high lift without any effect from recommending one product. Only the proposed randomized intervention can estimate incremental sales from the recommendation [4].

### Data issue, resolution, and limits

During the date reconstruction, **30 `InvoiceNo` values had more than one raw `InvoiceDate`**, at most one minute apart. Therefore, a one-timestamp-per-invoice assumption did not hold. The notebook assigned the earliest timestamp to each invoice, verified that each affected invoice stayed within one month, and confirmed an exact match of the rebuilt basket multiset to the app data. This resolves the split assignment for these periods but does not create timestamps in the exported app data.

The time benchmark favored FP-Growth, while its traced allocation was larger. The rule-screening choice reduced 950 rules at 1%/30% to 96 at 2%/30%, yet November showed that a useful aggregate rule can dip below the threshold. A next improvement is a genuinely prospective test: select a rule using data available at one cutoff, evaluate it on invoices collected strictly afterward, then run the controlled cross-sell if it still passes prespecified checks.

const patch = "*** Begin Patch
*** Delete File: /Users/raimova-al/Documents/study/master/res_sys/llm-4-res-sys/week4/raimova_alina_hw4_report.md
*** Add File: /Users/raimova-al/Documents/study/master/res_sys/llm-4-res-sys/week4/raimova_alina_hw4_report.md
+# Association Rules for Online Retail Baskets
+
+**Student:** Raimova Alina  
+**Team:** Individual  
+**Email:** aaraimova@edu.hse.ru  
+**Date:** 2026-10-06  
+**Assignment:** Association Rules (Week 4, HW4)  
+**Github link:** [Local repository remote](https://github.com/predprof/llm-4-res-sys) — student review required: confirm this is the submission repository and publish the Week 4 files.
+
+## Abstract
+
+This study asks whether products bought on the same invoice reveal useful retail association rules. It builds 17,080 invoice baskets from the UCI Online Retail data, implements FP-Growth in a browser app, and uses a notebook to compare Apriori, thresholds, and time periods. At 2% minimum support and 30% minimum confidence, 96 rules remain, all with lift above 1. A teacup rule is worth testing as a cross-sell recommendation, but historical co-purchases alone cannot establish that the recommendation will increase sales.
+
+**Index Terms -** association rules, market basket analysis, FP-Growth, Apriori, cross-sell
+
+## 1. Introduction
+
+**Problem statement.**
+
+The task is to turn invoice lines into baskets and find products bought together more often than expected. Each `InvoiceNo` is one transaction, `StockCode` identifies a product, and `Description` labels it. The app reports support, confidence, and lift for each selected rule.
+
+**Motivation.**
+
+A co-purchase count alone can be misleading when one product is common. A rule should be screened for both frequency and strength before a retailer considers a recommendation or bundle.
+
+**Concrete example.**
+
+Of 17,080 cleaned invoices, 541 contain both GREEN REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER [22697] and ROSES REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER [22699]. The analysis checks whether that pairing is strong enough to investigate and whether it persists later.
+
+**Contributions.**
+
+- Implement FP-Growth, rule generation, and support/confidence/lift display in the four-file browser app; its self-checks pass 11/11.
+- Compare Apriori and FP-Growth in a separate executed notebook, then examine thresholds, rule direction, and a historical time split.
+
+## 2. Related Work
+
+The UCI record defines the source fields and notes that many customers are wholesalers [1]. Apriori searches frequent itemsets with candidate generation and downward-closure pruning [2], while FP-Growth mines conditional FP-trees without Apriori's candidate-generation step [3]. Randomized online experiments can estimate whether a proposed recommendation changes behavior, unlike retrospective association analysis [4]. The official documentation for the notebook's tools is listed in [5]–[7].
+
+[1] D. Chen, “Online Retail,” *UCI Machine Learning Repository*, 2015, doi: 10.24432/C5BW33. [Online]. Available: [https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/352/online+retail](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/352/online+retail). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.
+
+[2] R. Agrawal and R. Srikant, “Fast Algorithms for Mining Association Rules in Large Databases,” in *Proc. 20th Int. Conf. Very Large Data Bases*, 1994, pp. 487–499. [Online]. Available: [https://www.vldb.org/conf/1994/P487.PDF](https://www.vldb.org/conf/1994/P487.PDF). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.
+
+[3] J. Han, J. Pei, and Y. Yin, “Mining Frequent Patterns without Candidate Generation,” in *Proc. ACM SIGMOD Int. Conf. Management of Data*, 2000. [Online]. Available: [https://sigmodrecord.org/publications/sigmodRecord/0006/pdfs/Mining%20Frequent%20Patterns%20without%20Candidate%20Generation.pdf](https://sigmodrecord.org/publications/sigmodRecord/0006/pdfs/Mining%20Frequent%20Patterns%20without%20Candidate%20Generation.pdf). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.
+
+[4] R. Kohavi, R. M. Henne, and D. Sommerfield, “Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HiPPO,” in *Proc. 13th ACM SIGKDD Int. Conf. Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining*, 2007. [Online]. Available: [https://ai.stanford.edu/~ronnyk/GuideControlledExperiments.pdf](https://ai.stanford.edu/~ronnyk/GuideControlledExperiments.pdf). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.
+
+[5] Python Software Foundation, “Python 3.13 Documentation.” [Online]. Available: [https://docs.python.org/3.13/](https://docs.python.org/3.13/). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.
+
+[6] pandas development team, “pandas Documentation.” [Online]. Available: [https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.
+
+[7] openpyxl project, “openpyxl Documentation.” [Online]. Available: [https://openpyxl.readthedocs.io/en/stable/](https://openpyxl.readthedocs.io/en/stable/). Accessed: Oct. 6, 2026.
+
+**Alternatives considered.**
+
+- **Apriori:** retained as a transparent baseline; it produced the same itemset counts as FP-Growth in the notebook.
+- **Confidence-only selection:** rejected because it ignores the consequent's base rate; lift supplies that comparison.
+
+## 3. Method
+
+**Approach.**
+
+The browser app mines frequent itemsets with FP-Growth and generates both directions of each nonempty rule split. For antecedent A, consequent B, and N baskets, support is `count(A∪B)/N`, confidence is `count(A∪B)/count(A)`, and lift is `confidence/[count(B)/N]`. Zero denominators produce an undefined metric rather than `NaN` or infinity.
+
+**Pipeline.**
+
+1. Start with the 541,909-row UCI workbook [1]. Remove cancellations and adjustments, nonpositive quantity or price, blank descriptions or customer IDs, and nonproduct codes; normalize stock codes and labels according to `readme.md`.
+2. Group by `InvoiceNo`, deduplicate `StockCode` within each invoice, and exclude baskets with fewer than two distinct items. The conceptual invoice–item matrix has **17,080 rows**, **3,653 product columns**, and **384,911 present invoice–item cells**; `transactions.js` stores it compactly.
+3. Mine itemsets, generate directed rules, and report their counts and metrics. Screen at support **≥2%** (at least **342** joint invoices), confidence **≥30%**, and lift **>1**.
+4. Reconstruct dated baskets from the original workbook's `InvoiceDate` and compare January–August 2011 with September–November 2011. The app export has no dates, so the notebook uses the original dates; none were simulated.
+
+**Tools and libraries.**
+
+- Plain browser JavaScript runs the four-file app without a build step; the browser version was not recorded.
+- Python **3.13.7** [5] runs the analysis notebook and mining benchmarks.
+- pandas **3.0.3** [6] and openpyxl **3.1.5** [7] read and clean the original workbook for the time check.
+
+**Key design decisions.**
+
+- **Basket identity:** one `InvoiceNo` is one transaction, and repeated stock lines count once; this measures invoice co-occurrence, not quantities sold.
+- **Thresholds:** 2% support keeps at least 342 joint invoices, while 30% confidence leaves 96 rules to inspect; the notebook's sweep shows how looser and stricter values change that number.
+- **Time check:** the teacup rule was chosen on the full dataset before its later-period check; other product checks are exploratory and are not substituted after seeing the results.
+
+**Configuration.**
+
+The notebook used the same 17,080 loaded baskets for both algorithms. Its 1% benchmark requires 171 baskets, uses deterministic item ordering and no random seed, alternates method order over five timing repeats, and excludes data loading. Peak `tracemalloc` allocation is measured in separate runs, not as total process RAM. The notebook ran on Darwin; CPU and total RAM were not recorded. December 2010 and incomplete December 2011 are excluded from the two full-month comparison periods.
+
+## 4. Experiments
+
+### 4.1 Apriori versus FP-Growth
+
+**Setup.**
+
+The executed notebook compared its posting-set Apriori implementation with its FP-tree implementation on the same baskets at 1% support. Mining time is the median of five runs; traced peak allocation comes from a separate run. The browser app's 11 self-checks were also rerun against its five-basket fixture.
+
+**Results.**
+
+**Table 1. Frequent-itemset benchmark at 1% support.**
+
+| Algorithm | Itemsets | Median time | Peak traced allocation |
+|---|---:|---:|---:|
+| Apriori | 1,219 | 1.899 s | 28.6 MiB |
+| FP-Growth | 1,219 | 1.103 s | 59.5 MiB |
+
+Both methods returned exactly the same itemsets and counts. FP-Growth was faster in this run, while Apriori used less traced memory; the comparison is specific to these Python implementations. The browser app's self-checks passed **11/11**.
+
+### 4.2 Thresholds, useful and misleading rules, and direction
+
+**Setup.**
+
+The notebook first mined at 0.5% support, then applied several support and confidence filters to the same candidate rules. The chosen screen was 2% support, 30% confidence, and lift >1. Rule counts come from the notebook; the three rule examples were also checked against the app's basket counts.
+
+**Results.**
+
+At 0.5% support, the notebook found 5,255 itemsets and 21,026 possible directed rules. Its histograms show **20,918** candidate rules below 2% support and **10,303** below 30% confidence. Table 2 shows the trade-off; every listed rule had lift >1.
+
+**Table 2. Threshold sweep from the notebook.**
+
+| Support | Confidence | Itemsets | Rules |
+|---:|---:|---:|---:|
+| 0.5% | 30% | 5,255 | 10,723 |
+| 1% | 30% | 1,219 | 950 |
+| 2% | 30% | 294 | 96 |
+| 3% | 30% | 115 | 12 |
+| 2% | 60% | 294 | 20 |
+
+Raising support removes rare itemsets and their possible rules because a superset cannot be more frequent than its subsets. Raising confidence leaves the itemsets unchanged but removes weaker directions. Lower thresholds reveal more niche combinations and more noise; higher thresholds are easier to review but may hide useful niche patterns. The 2%/30% setting is a practical screening choice, not a universal optimum.
+
+**Table 3. Useful and misleading examples across all 17,080 baskets.** Counts are invoices, not units.
+
+| Judgment and rule | count(A) | count(B) | Both | Support | Confidence | Lift |
+|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
+| **Investigate:** GREEN REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER [22697] → ROSES REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER [22699] | 691 | 780 | 541 | 3.17% | 78.29% | 17.14 |
+| **Reject:** ALARM CLOCK BAKELIKE RED [22727] → WHITE HANGING HEART T-LIGHT HOLDER [85123A] | 877 | 1,959 | 98 | 0.57% | 11.17% | 0.97 |
+
+The teacup pair has 541 joint invoices, passes the screen, and has lift far above 1, so it is worth investigating as a cross-sell. The clock-to-holder rule has 98 co-purchases but fails all three filters. The holder occurs in **11.47%** of all baskets, slightly *more* than its **11.17%** confidence after a red clock; the raw co-purchase count is therefore misleading. Because even the most common item occurs in only 11.47% of baskets, these data do not provide a high-confidence, near-unit-lift rule among the chosen high-confidence rules.
+
+For rule direction, **JUMBO BAG PINK POLKADOT [22386] → JUMBO BAG RED RETROSPOT [85099B]** has confidence **546/869 = 62.83%**. Reverse it and confidence becomes **546/1,584 = 34.47%**. Both directions have **3.20% support** and **6.77 lift**: the shared numerator is unchanged, but confidence uses a different antecedent count.
+
+As a transparent metric check, the teacup support is `541/17,080 = 3.1674%`, confidence is `541/691 = 78.2923%`, and lift is `(541/691)/(780/17,080) = 17.1440`. These inputs matched direct app counts; **student review required:** recalculate at least one result personally before submission.
+
+### 4.3 Later-period validation and intervention plan
+
+**Setup.**
+
+The notebook rebuilt dated baskets from the original workbook and confirmed their multiset exactly matches `transactions.js`. It checked the preselected teacup rule in January–August 2011 versus September–November 2011; 1,981 invoices in December 2010 and December 2011 lie outside those full-month periods. Other product pairs were checked only as exploratory comparisons.
+
+**Results.**
+
+**Table 4. Teacup rule in earlier and later full-month periods.**
+
+| Period | Baskets | Green A | Roses B | Both | Support | Confidence | Lift |
+|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
+| Jan–Aug 2011 | 9,220 | 448 | 506 | 360 | 3.90% | 80.36% | 14.64 |
+| Sep–Nov 2011 | 5,879 | 192 | 218 | 144 | 2.45% | 75.00% | 20.23 |
+
+The aggregate later period still passes 2% support, 30% confidence, and lift >1, with 144 joint invoices. Confidence fell **5.36 percentage points**; its approximate 95% change interval is **−12.50 to +1.79 points**, so a drop exceeding 10 points cannot be ruled out. November alone had **1.70% support**, below the threshold. This is a retrospective check, not an independent held-out evaluation, because the rule was selected using the full dataset. Exploratory checks found pink → red jumbo-bag confidence of 63.35% earlier and 62.32% later, while red → green alarm-clock confidence rose from 48.77% to 72.24%.
+
+A controlled cross-sell test would randomly assign eligible customers, after they add the green teacup without the roses teacup, 50/50 to control or treatment. Treatment shows the roses teacup in the existing recommendation slot; control shows the current item in that slot, with identical prices and promotions. The primary outcome is roses-teacup purchases per eligible checkout, with gross margin, green-teacup checkout completion, and returns as guardrails. A pilot should estimate the eligible-session baseline and set sample size for 80% power against a prespecified business-relevant effect; deploy only if the planned run gives an incremental attach-rate 95% interval above zero without material guardrail harm [4]. **No live experiment was run.** The observed 75% basket confidence is not an eligible-session control rate because the dataset does not record add-to-cart order.
+
+## 5. Discussion
+
+**Failure case.**
+
+Date reconstruction found **30 `InvoiceNo` values with more than one `InvoiceDate`**, at most one minute apart. Therefore, assigning an invoice date by assuming every line has the same timestamp would be unsafe.
+
+**Root cause.**
+
+The raw workbook records line-level timestamps, and those 30 invoices contain more than one timestamp. The evidence identifies this inconsistency; it does not establish why those timestamps differ.
+
+**Fix and verification.**
+
+The notebook assigns the earliest timestamp to each invoice, verifies that all affected invoices remain in the same month, and confirms that the reconstructed basket multiset exactly matches the app data. The later-period split therefore uses real source dates without changing basket membership.
+
+**What worked.**
+
+- FP-Growth and Apriori produced identical 1% itemsets; the 2%/30% screen reduced 950 rules at 1%/30% to 96 with at least 342 joint invoices each.
+- Lift helped reject a co-purchase count that looked substantial in isolation. Lift **17.14** for the teacups means roughly 17 times the co-occurrence expected under independence, **not** 17 times more sales from a recommendation. Wholesalers may buy matching colors, or shared promotion and placement may explain the association. A randomized test is needed to estimate an intervention's causal effect [4].
+
+**What surprised me or did not work.**
+
+- The later-period aggregate teacup rule passed, but November support fell below 2%; the selected rule is not stable by every month. FP-Growth also used more traced memory despite its shorter mining time.
+- **Student review required:** state in your own words what surprised you, whether you agree with this interpretation, which alternative you considered, and one result you personally checked. A prospective rule-selection cutoff followed by genuinely future invoices would improve the stability test.
+
+## 6. AI Usage Disclosure
+
+- **AI tools used:** Codex desktop agent; exact model/version and any other tools require confirmation from the authentic session export.
+- **How AI was used:** assisted with JavaScript implementation, notebook analysis and debugging, interpretation, reference checks, and this report draft.
+- **What I personally verified:** **Student review required:** include only a calculation, rerun, or source check you actually performed yourself; the arithmetic in §4.2 is available to check.
+- **What I trusted without full verification:** **Student review required:** state any AI-assisted results you did not check. This draft claims no student verification.
+- **Session log reference:** The authentic `raimova_alina_hw4_session.json` export is **not attached to this draft**. Add only the unmodified tool-native export; do not reconstruct it.
+
+## References
+
+See §2 (numbered [1]–[7]).
*** End Patch";

 **Approach.**
 
-[Describe the approach in 2-4 sentences.]
+The browser app mines frequent itemsets with FP-Growth and generates both directions of each nonempty rule split. For antecedent A, consequent B, and N baskets, support is `count(A∪B)/N`, confidence is `count(A∪B)/count(A)`, and lift is `confidence/[count(B)/N]`. Zero denominators produce an undefined metric rather than `NaN` or infinity.
@@
-[Insert a labeled diagram or numbered pipeline.]
+1. Start with the 541,909-row UCI workbook [1]. Remove cancellations and adjustments, nonpositive quantity or price, blank descriptions or customer IDs, and nonproduct codes; normalize stock codes and labels according to `readme.md`.
+2. Group by `InvoiceNo`, deduplicate `StockCode` within each invoice, and exclude baskets with fewer than two distinct items. The conceptual invoice–item matrix has **17,080 rows**, **3,653 product columns**, and **384,911 present invoice–item cells**; `transactions.js` stores it compactly.
+3. Mine itemsets, generate directed rules, and report their counts and metrics. Screen at support **≥2%** (at least **342** joint invoices), confidence **≥30%**, and lift **>1**.
+4. Reconstruct dated baskets from the original workbook's `InvoiceDate` and compare January–August 2011 with September–November 2011. The app export has no dates, so the notebook uses the original dates; none were simulated.
@@

### 4.3 Later-period validation and intervention plan

**Setup.**

The notebook rebuilt dated baskets from the original workbook and confirmed their multiset exactly matches `transactions.js`. It checked the preselected teacup rule in January–August 2011 versus September–November 2011; 1,981 invoices in December 2010 and December 2011 lie outside those full-month periods. **Results.**

**Table 4. Teacup rule in earlier and later full-month periods.**

| Period | Baskets | Green A | Roses B | Both | Support | Confidence | Lift |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jan–Aug 2011 | 9,220 | 448 | 506 | 360 | 3.90% | 80.36% | 14.64 |
| Sep–Nov 2011 | 5,879 | 192 | 218 | 144 | 2.45% | 75.00% | 20.23 |

The aggregate later period still passes 2% support, 30% confidence, and lift >1, with 144 joint invoices. Confidence fell **5.36 percentage points**; its approximate 95% change interval is **−12.50 to +1.79 points**, so a drop exceeding 10 points cannot be ruled out. November alone had **1.70% support**, below the threshold. This is a retrospective check, not an independent held-out evaluation, because the rule was selected using the full dataset. Exploratory checks found pink → red jumbo-bag confidence of 63.35% earlier and 62.32% later, while red → green alarm-clock confidence rose from 48.77% to 72.24%.

A controlled cross-sell test would randomly assign eligible customers, after they add the green teacup without the roses teacup, 50/50 to control or treatment. Treatment shows the roses teacup in the existing recommendation slot; control shows the current item in that slot, with identical prices and promotions. The primary outcome is roses-teacup purchases per eligible checkout, with gross margin, green-teacup checkout completion, and returns as guardrails. A pilot should estimate the eligible-session baseline and set sample size for 80% power against a prespecified business-relevant effect; deploy only if the planned run gives an incremental attach-rate 95% interval above zero without material guardrail harm [4]. **No live experiment was run.** The observed 75% basket confidence is not an eligible-session control rate because the dataset does not record add-to-cart order.

# Content-Based Movie Recommender

Homework 2 project built with the MovieLens 100K dataset. The application recommends Top-5 unseen movies using genre features and displays a score for every result.

**[Open the live demo](https://predprof.github.io/movie-recommender-system/)**

## Recommendation modes

- Item-to-item cosine similarity
- Item-to-item Jaccard similarity
- Profile-based cosine similarity using a user's three top-rated movies
- Single-item vs. aggregated-profile comparison with a chronological 5-star holdout

## Run locally

Start a static web server in this directory:

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8000
```

Then open [http://localhost:8000](http://localhost:8000).

*** Update File: /Users/raimova-al/Documents/study/master/res_sys/hw-repo/products-association-rules/README.md
@@
-# products-association-rules
-Association Rules
+# Product Association Rules
+
+Homework 4 project using the [UCI Online Retail dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/352/online+retail). Each invoice is a basket; the app uses FP-Growth to find frequent product groups and shows association rules with support, confidence, and lift.
+
+**[Open the live demo](https://predprof.github.io/products-association-rules/)**
+
+## Features
+
+- Adjust minimum support and confidence.
+- Inspect a rule and compare its reverse direction.
+- Run the built-in self-checks.
+
+## Run locally
+
+Open `index.html` in a modern browser. Keep `transactions.js`, `script.js`, and `style.css` in the same directory.

name: "pdf"
description: "Read, create, inspect, render, and verify PDF files where visual layout matters, including fillable AcroForms. Use Poppler rendering plus Python tools such as reportlab, pdfplumber, and pypdf for generation and extraction."
---

# PDF Skill

## When To Use

- Read or review PDF content where layout and visuals matter.
- Create PDFs programmatically with reliable formatting.
- Fill and validate interactive PDF forms.
- Validate final rendering before delivery.

## Tools + Contract Requirements

Immediately before the first create/edit authoring command, run `mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs` successfully exactly once using the command below. Do not run it for read-only work. For edits, replace `create` with `edit`; adjust the expected count and output format to match the requested outputs.



```bash
node container_tools/mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs --operation-kind create --expected-output-count 1 --output-format pdf
```

## Workflow

1. Prefer visual review: render PDF pages to PNGs and inspect them.
   - Use `pdftoppm` from the bundled runtime or system Poppler when available.
   - If unavailable, install Poppler or ask the user to review the output locally.
2. Use `reportlab` to generate PDFs when creating new documents.
3. Use `pdfplumber` or `pypdf` for text extraction and quick checks; do not rely on text extraction for layout fidelity.
4. After each meaningful update, re-render pages and verify alignment, spacing, and legibility.

## Fill And Validate AcroForms

Visual review alone is not a correctness check for a fillable PDF. A page `/Widget` annotation can render a value from its appearance stream while the canonical `/AcroForm/Fields` tree is missing or contains a stale value.

1. Keep the result interactive by default; set `flatten=True` only when the user explicitly requests a completed, static form. Preserve the source PDF, and do not flatten a signed PDF without an explicit workflow decision.
2. Inspect both representations before filling: enumerate fields from `reader.get_fields()` and `/Widget` annotations from every page's `/Annots`, following `/Parent` and `/Kids`. If a widget and a canonical field have the same name but are distinct objects with no `/Parent` relationship, do not call `reattach_fields()` blindly: it can create a second top-level field with the same name. Report the ambiguity or produce a static result.
3. Recover genuinely orphaned widgets, fill all pages, and write the result with `pypdf`:

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter
from pypdf.generic import NameObject

reader = PdfReader(input_pdf)
writer = PdfWriter()
writer.clone_document_from_reader(reader)

# Restores widgets that are missing from /AcroForm/Fields.
writer.reattach_fields()
fields = writer.get_fields() or {}
missing = set(expected_values) - set(fields)
if missing:
    raise ValueError(f"Form fields not found after repair: {sorted(missing)}")

values_to_write = dict(expected_values)
if flatten:
    # Paint every existing value before removing every widget.
    values_to_write = {
        name: field.get("/V", "/Off" if field.get("/FT") == "/Btn" else "")
        for name, field in fields.items()
    }
    values_to_write.update(expected_values)

writer.update_page_form_field_values(
    None, values_to_write, auto_regenerate=False, flatten=flatten
)

if flatten:
    # pypdf's flatten=True paints appearances but does not remove widgets.
    writer.remove_annotations(subtypes="/Widget")
    writer.root_object.pop(NameObject("/AcroForm"), None)

with open(output_pdf, "wb") as stream:
    writer.write(stream)
```

4. Reopen the written PDF before delivery. For an interactive result, require every expected field to be present in `get_fields()` with the expected `/V`, enumerate page widgets again, and confirm their effective `/V` (the widget value or inherited `/Parent` value) agrees. Confirm each updated widget has a non-empty `/AP` `/N` appearance and render the final pages to catch stale or clipped appearances. Do not rely on `/NeedAppearances` or a successful PNG render as proof that logical field data was updated.
5. For a flattened result, require zero `/Widget` annotations and no remaining `/AcroForm` field tree after reopening, then render the final pages. Keep an editable copy when the user may need to revise the form.

## Temp And Output Conventions

- Use `tmp/pdfs/` for intermediate files; delete them when done.
- Write final artifacts under `output/pdf/` when working in this repo.
- Keep filenames stable and descriptive.

## Dependencies

Prefer the Codex bundled workspace/runtime dependencies when available. The primary runtime is expected to include:

- Python packages: `reportlab`, `pdfplumber`, `pypdf`
- Rendering tools: `pdftoppm` and `pdfinfo` from Poppler

If a dependency is missing, install only what is needed.

Python packages:

```bash
uv pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```

If `uv` is unavailable:

```bash
python3 -m pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```

System tools for rendering:

```bash
# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install poppler

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install -y poppler-utils
```

If installation is not possible in this environment, tell the user which dependency is missing and how to install it locally.

## Environment

No required environment variables.

## Rendering Command

```bash
pdftoppm -png "$INPUT_PDF" "$OUTPUT_PREFIX"
```

## Quality Expectations

- Maintain polished visual design: consistent typography, spacing, margins, and section hierarchy.
- Avoid rendering issues: clipped text, overlapping elements, broken tables, black squares, or unreadable glyphs.
- Charts, tables, and images must be sharp, aligned, and clearly labeled.
- Use ASCII hyphens only. Avoid U+2011 and other Unicode dashes.
- Citations and references must be human-readable; never leave tool tokens or placeholder strings.

## Final Checks

- Do not deliver until the latest PNG inspection shows zero visual or formatting defects.
- Confirm headers, footers, page numbering, and section transitions look polished.
- Keep intermediate files organized or remove them after final approval.

## Final response

### Final Response Citations

- **Create/edit:** for created or edited PDFs, cite each final deliverable exactly once with `purpose="output"`, in its own paragraph. Briefly describe the result without repeating its filename, path, or link. Never put output directives inside prose or list items.
- **Q&A and summaries:** Every file whose contents you summarize or use to support an answer MUST receive a `:codex-file-citation{...}` with `purpose="source"` in the final response. Use the source citation in place of the filename, wherever the filename would appear. Do not write the filename separately and append its citation at the end. Files merely inspected but not used in the answer need no citation. Do not emit output citations for unchanged files or read-only answers.

- Emit `:codex-file-citation{...}` directly, without backticks, code fences, or a Markdown-link wrapper. Use verified targets only. No need to cite or reference intermediate work.

For file citations, set `path` to the verified absolute file path on the task host. Omit `mode`.

Some illustrative examples, real responses use verified targets outside code fences.

```text
:codex-file-citation{path="/absolute/path/review.pdf" purpose="output"}
```

```text
The review of :codex-file-citation{path="/absolute/path/review.pdf" purpose="source"} is due Friday.
```


### Additional Citation Guidance

For PDF Q&A, inspect complete relevant pages and preserve material headings, table/figure labels, footnotes, sources, and sample sizes. PDF citations support only plain file citations; do not add `artifact_kind`, `page_number`, or other locators.
